title: Outposts: what flips the verdict
outcomes: Predicts whether removing the supporting pawn or adding a lever pawn changes an outpost verdict
Names the pawn that supports the square or the pawn that could attack it
States, on paper, one reason for and one reason against trading the outpost piece (unchecked by the app)

steps.text: This lesson builds on **Outposts: a square no pawn can reach** and **Is it a real outpost? Two checks, any piece**. An outpost lives or dies by its pawns. Change one pawn and the verdict can flip: the supporting pawn steps away, or an enemy pawn arrives that can come forward as a *lever* against the square. Predict each flip before you check.

steps.title: Supporting pawn on d4 or on e4
steps.prompt: Only one White pawn differs. Is c5 an outpost square for White in the second position? Predict, then check.

steps.title: A lever pawn
steps.prompt: Only one Black pawn differs. Is d6 an outpost square for White in the second position? Predict, then check.

steps.text: Two ways the verdict flips. **The supporter changes:** a pawn that moves to another file may no longer defend the square. **A lever appears:** an enemy pawn on a neighbouring file that has not yet passed the attacking rank can still come forward to attack the piece. *Rule of thumb:* check both pawns whenever a pawn move changes the position near the outpost.

Should you trade the piece on an outpost? There is no checked rule for it yet. Treat these lines as a *rule of thumb*, and use the paper exercise at the end to test it. A piece that cannot be driven away is worth keeping while it has targets. If it is hitting nothing, trading it may be right. The app does not check this.

steps.prompt: Pick an outpost knight from one of your own games, or imagine one. List what it attacks from there. Would you trade it? Write one reason for and one against, and say what you would look at to decide. This is a paper exercise; nothing here checks the trade decision.
